item.title: Building an engineering plugin for GitHub Copilot
item.description: Package engineering skills for GitHub Copilot in VS Code, the Copilot app, and CLI, using Git-Ape as an example and evaluating skills against realistic tasks.
item.content:encoded:
Reviewing a Terraform plan, checking deployment prerequisites, or assessing Azure policies: these are tasks we repeat across projects. We usually have a process for each one, spread across documentation, scripts, and repository instructions.

GitHub Copilot plugins give us a way to package those practices and share them with an engineering team, whether we work in VS Code, the GitHub Copilot app, or Copilot CLI. A plugin can include skills, agents, hooks, and MCP server configuration. In this post, we will use Git-Ape as a concrete example, look at a simplified engineering skill, and see how to evaluate whether it is actually helping.

Engineering plugins series: 1. Build and evaluate | 2. Distribute to the team (coming soon) | 3. Manage across the enterprise (coming soon)

Technical references checked October 24, 2026. The examples below are based on documentation and source review; the installation and evaluation steps have not been reproduced end to end.

Where can we use plugins?​

We can use the plugin package from several Copilot clients:

ClientWhere to start
VS CodeDiscover agent plugins in the Extensions view with @agentPlugins.
GitHub Copilot appOpen Customize > Plugins to browse marketplaces and install plugins.
Copilot CLIUse the plugin commands shown later in this walkthrough.

GitHub also supports plugins in Copilot cloud agent through repository configuration. See the VS Code plugin guide for editor-specific discovery and installation.

The Copilot app's plugin inventory. Browse shows available plugins; Installed shows packages already present. Screenshots in this series show the app as captured in October 2026.

Check the plugin's supported components, required tools, and authentication in each client. GitHub's plugin overview documents the supported surfaces and installation entry points.

For this walkthrough, we will use CLI commands for local installation and an SDK-based harness for automated evaluations. We will also look at what to check separately in VS Code and the app.

Choose one task and establish a baseline​

Before writing a skill, try the workflow without it. Give Copilot a few representative tasks and observe where it struggles, asks for missing context, or produces an inconsistent result. This gives you a baseline and helps you target the actual gap instead of adding instructions for a problem you may not have.

Write down what a good result should do, then create a small set of realistic cases. Include tasks where the skill should apply, nearby tasks where it should not, and cases with missing or ambiguous input. For example, a Terraform plan review might include:

Add a destructive-change case too: a plan that deletes a resource containing persistent data should prompt an evidence-based discussion of data loss and recovery, not just a count of deleted resources.

Note the behaviors that matter: identify the affected resource, explain risks using evidence in the plan, ask for missing information, and stay within the requested task. These baseline cases will help you see whether the skill improves the outcome and whether the improvement persists after later edits.

Use Git-Ape as a reference​

A narrow skill with clear expectations is easier to test than a generic instruction such as "be a better engineer." Once it is useful, a plugin gives us a way to package and maintain it alongside related capabilities.

To make this concrete, we will use Git-Ape, an engineering plugin for Azure deployment workflows. Git-Ape is experimental and not production-ready; use a sandbox when trying it. The manifest reviewed here uses the legacy Copilot format, with component paths under .github/. Copilot CLI also supports Agent Plugins 1.0, a portable format for skills and MCP servers. Choose one format and follow its documented locations.

The Agent Skills specification defines the skill folder itself: a SKILL.md file with optional scripts and references. The plugin manifest adds packaging and installation metadata around those capabilities.

Already have an AGENTS.md? Start there​

You do not need to replace your repository instructions to use a plugin. Keep project-specific guidance in AGENTS.md or .github/copilot-instructions.md: how to build and test, where the important code lives, and which files should not be edited.

A skill describes how to perform a particular task. A custom agent defines a specialized role and its configuration. A plugin packages reusable capabilities so you can share and maintain them across projects. For example, repository instructions can say that infrastructure changes need validation, while a shared plugin supplies the validation workflow.

The filenames matter: AGENTS.md is an instruction file; .github/agents/reviewer.agent.md is a custom agent definition. A file literally named agent.md is not automatically either one. Supported instruction filenames and scope vary by client and feature; see GitHub's custom instructions overview and instruction support matrix.

Extract a reusable workflow into a skill and keep local project conventions in repository instructions. That gives each rule one place to maintain. Mentioning a skill in AGENTS.md does not install it; the plugin still needs to be available in the client.

GitHub's customization comparison describes these roles in more detail. Its Agent Skills announcement also explains how skills load when relevant to a task.

What goes into a plugin?​

Skills capture task-specific instructions and supporting material. Agents define a more specialized assistant, hooks run at lifecycle events, and MCP server configuration connects the client to external tools. Start with the smallest set of components that solves the workflow.

Git-Ape's structure shows how a plugin can grow from a manifest and skills into a maintained engineering toolkit:

git-ape/
├── plugin.json
└── .github/
    ├── agents/
    ├── prompts/
    ├── skills/
    │   ├── azure-policy-advisor/
    │   │   ├── SKILL.md
    │   │   ├── references/
    │   │   └── scripts/
    │   └── azure-stack-deploy/
    │       ├── SKILL.md
    │       └── scripts/
    └── evals/                  # Repository tests, not a runtime component
        └── azure-policy-advisor/
            ├── eval.yaml
            └── tasks/

Here is a shortened version of Git-Ape's manifest, showing its component paths:

{
  "name": "git-ape",
  "agents": ".github/agents/",
  "skills": ".github/skills/",
  "prompts": ".github/prompts/"
}

For the supported plugin.json fields, see GitHub's CLI manifest reference. For the portable format and client-specific components, see the shared plugin manifest reference.

This manifest has no Agent Plugins 1.0 $schema, so it uses the legacy format and its configurable paths. For a new portable plugin, include the canonical schema in plugin.json; put skills in immediate subdirectories of a root skills/ directory, and MCP configuration in a root mcp.json. Copilot-specific components then live under com.github.copilot/. See the plugin creation guide for the exact structure.

Add a skill​

In the Git-Ape layout, a skill starts at .github/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md. Git-Ape's azure-policy-advisor is a real example: its skill instructions are supported by focused reference files and a script. The following Terraform plan review skill is a separate, simplified illustration—not a skill from Git-Ape:

---
name: terraform-plan-review
description: Review a Terraform plan for security, reliability, and unintended infrastructure changes before it is applied.
---

# Terraform plan review

When asked to review a Terraform plan:

1. Read the plan output and identify additions, changes, and deletions.
2. Highlight changes that affect identity, network exposure, encryption,
   backups, availability, or data retention.
3. Explain the impact of each finding and cite the relevant resource or
   plan detail.
4. Separate confirmed risks from questions that need more context.
5. Summarize the findings by severity and recommend what to verify next.

Do not run `terraform apply`. If the plan or required context is missing,
ask for it instead of guessing.

The skill's description helps Copilot determine when the instructions are relevant. Keep it specific enough to distinguish this workflow from general Terraform questions. The body describes the process, required evidence, and boundaries, including the instruction to leave the infrastructure unchanged. GitHub's skill authoring guide documents the required frontmatter and skill selection.

To try this example without changing Git-Ape, create a separate terraform-review directory. Save the skill above as .github/skills/terraform-plan-review/SKILL.md inside it, and add this legacy-format plugin.json at its root:

{
  "name": "terraform-review",
  "skills": ".github/skills/"
}

Avoid turning the skill into a handbook. Put only the instructions needed to complete the workflow in SKILL.md; link or include additional reference material when the workflow genuinely needs it.

Install and try it locally with the CLI​

With Copilot CLI installed and signed in, run the following from the parent directory of your Git-Ape checkout:

copilot plugin install ./git-ape
copilot plugin list

Start a new interactive Copilot CLI session and check that the skill is available:

/skills list

For Git-Ape, try a read-only prerequisite check with /prereq-check, explicitly asking it to report missing tools without installing anything or deploying resources.

For our Terraform example, run this from the parent directory of terraform-review, then start a new session:

copilot plugin install ./terraform-review

Provide a representative plan and check that the response identifies changes, explains impact, separates evidence from assumptions, and leaves the infrastructure unchanged.

One detail is easy to miss while iterating: for this direct local installation, the authoring guide says components are cached. After changing the plugin, install it again before testing the changes in a new session:

copilot plugin install ./git-ape

This is not a rule for every local source: the CLI reference separately documents live loading for path-sourced plugins in a directory-source marketplace, with changes picked up on restart or a new session.

When you are finished, remove the local installation with the plugin's manifest name:

copilot plugin uninstall git-ape

For the Terraform example, use copilot plugin uninstall terraform-review.

Evaluate the skill, not just the installation​

Seeing the skill in /skills list confirms that the client can discover it. Now we need to check its behavior: does it follow the process, produce useful findings, and stay within the task?

The same distinction applies in the app. Here, Git-Ape appears with its version, marketplace source, and enabled toggle:

This confirms the plugin is enabled. To see whether a skill actually ran, we need to inspect a task session.

Git-Ape keeps evaluations next to the plugin in .github/evals/. These files are not plugin runtime components; they are a separate test harness. Git-Ape uses Waza to define an evaluation suite and the tasks it runs. Its azure-policy-advisor suite and task files include cases such as:

ScenarioWhat a good result should do
A user asks for a CIS Azure compliance auditTrigger the skill and address the framework, resource types, initiative-versus-policy choice, and an audit-first rollout.
A user asks an unrelated Linux kernel questionDo not trigger Azure Policy guidance; answer the Linux question or acknowledge that it is outside the skill's scope.
A user asks a naming or cost questionKeep the policy-advisor skill quiet so the relevant skill or general Copilot behavior can handle it.

These cases target two different questions: is the skill relevant to the prompt, and is the resulting answer good? Git-Ape uses a heuristic trigger grader for relevance, and prompt graders for answer criteria and out-of-scope behavior.

The distinction is important: Waza's trigger grader scores keyword overlap and trigger-phrase matches against the skill text. It does not observe or prove actual skill invocation. Treat that score as a relevance check, then inspect skill-loading and tool-call evidence in real client sessions to test routing. A manually invoked skill tests its workflow, not whether Copilot would select it automatically.

For a real evaluation, give each task a stable input and an explicit rubric. For example, the CIS audit task checks that the answer acknowledges the requested benchmark, explains the initiative-versus-individual-policy trade-off, recommends an audit-first rollout, and touches multiple resource categories. The negative Linux task checks that the response does not wander into Azure governance.

Install Waza using its installation guide, configure authentication for the real-model executor, and check that the suite's configured model is available to your account. Then run the suite from the Git-Ape repository with:

waza run .github/evals/azure-policy-advisor/eval.yaml -v

Waza is a separate evaluation tool. This suite uses a configured Copilot SDK executor and model, runs multiple trials, and sets timeouts. Real-model evaluations may consume premium requests; check the suite configuration and your organization's usage settings before running it or adding it to CI. Mock execution is useful for checking the harness setup, but provides no evidence of real-model answer quality.

Use the same cases when comparing a skill revision with the previous version. Exact wording is usually a poor pass/fail condition for a generative response. Check the behavior that matters, and inspect grader judgments rather than treating a score as ground truth. A score can hide gaps in the test cases or a grader that is checking the wrong thing. Record the skill revision, client and harness versions, model, and relevant settings for each run so that results can be compared fairly.

Include checks in every client your engineers use: install through VS Code's agent-plugin interface or the app's Customize > Plugins, run the same positive, negative, and missing-input cases, and inspect the responses and tool calls. The SDK evaluation above does not drive those interfaces or verify their installation flows. Keep client-specific checks separate from the automated skill scores.

You do not need a full harness to get started. A small set of positive, negative, and edge-case prompts with written pass criteria is already more useful than testing only the happy path. Git-Ape's evaluation files are a good example of how to grow that practice into a repeatable suite and CI check.

Add capabilities only when they are needed​

Once the skill works, you can extend the plugin. The paths below are for Agent Plugins 1.0, not Git-Ape's legacy layout:

  • Add a custom agent under com.github.copilot/agents/ when the task benefits from a distinct role and configured tools.
  • Add hooks under com.github.copilot/hooks/ for lifecycle checks that need deterministic execution.
  • Add mcp.json at the plugin root when the workflow needs an external system through an MCP server.

Keep access narrow. Review a plugin's instructions, scripts, hooks, and MCP connections before installing or sharing it, especially when it comes from a source you do not control. Avoid pre-approving shell or bash tools unless you have audited the skill and its scripts: GitHub warns that doing so can allow attacker-controlled instructions to run arbitrary commands. Never put credentials in plugin files, and do not grant tools the workflow does not need. See GitHub's script security guidance and Anthropic's Agent Skills security considerations.

Now it’s your turn​

Start by testing one repeated engineering task and recording what is missing. Capture a few realistic cases, package the needed instructions as a skill, then rerun the same cases after each change. Share the plugin only after reviewing the code and connections it brings into the engineering environment.

That gives us a first skill, a plugin to carry it, and cases to check whether it helps. In the next article, we will make the package available to a team and manage its updates.

Happy building, and let me know which workflows you are turning into skills!

Arnaud

item.title: Building and shipping AzureCAF 2.0.0 with GitHub Copilot
item.description: How Copilot clients, cloud agents, proactive workflows, maintainer briefings, and GitHub security fit into AzureCAF delivery, with a candid look at the numbers.
item.content:encoded:
Before the 2.0 release, one Copilot-assisted update expanded AzureCAF's resource catalog by 22%. The initial proposal was marked ready for review 43 minutes after assignment; the reviewed change became available in a release about 11 days after the PR opened.

Preparing AzureCAF 2.0.0, published on October 19, 2026, gave us a chance to improve the whole delivery process: discovering work, preparing changes, keeping maintainers informed, and getting a release out safely.

Testing was a particularly useful application of AI: we could expand the checks, investigate failures, and build release confidence over successive iterations.

The provider generates Azure resource names in Terraform. Its history gives us a practical case study in AI-assisted development, community contributions, and the maintainer time needed to bring them together.

One repository connects the work​

I use Copilot through the CLI, Visual Studio Code, and the desktop app for interactive work. The cloud agent handles delegated tasks, preparing changes in a cloud environment and bringing them back for review.

GitHub Agentic Workflows runs recurring research and event-driven tasks. Findings, proposed changes, test results, and maintainer reports come back into the same repository.

Shared issues, PRs, and checks connect the tools with maintainer decisions. Illustrations use GitHub Octicons; editable diagram source.

Before delegating, I want a clear task, an expected result, and a way to check it. A cloud agent can work on a bounded change while I investigate another problem locally. The PR becomes the handoff: a diff, supporting sources, and evidence from the checks. Release approval remains a maintainer decision.

Shared repository skills give agents the research and testing procedures behind that handoff.

AzureCAF context: naming, usage, and the 2.0.0 changes

Back in 2021, I wrote about my first contribution to AzureCAF: naming support for Azure Dedicated Hosts. As Azure added services, researching new entries and maintaining existing definitions became a growing part of our work.

The AzureCAF provider generates names using resource-specific Azure naming rules and CAF abbreviations. It handles differences in allowed characters, length, prefixes, suffixes, and random characters across a catalog of 520 definitions.

A shared Terraform naming module can also centralize rules, be versioned, and calculate names offline during planning. We use AzureCAF for its maintained catalog and the implementation and tests behind it. Teams can reuse that work across their Terraform configurations.

ConsiderationNaming inside each resource moduleShared naming moduleAzureCAF provider
Rule ownershipEach module maintains its rulesOne reusable module maintains the rulesOne provider maintains a resource-specific catalog
ConsistencyDepends on keeping implementations alignedShared implementation; callers select module versionsShared implementation; Terraform resolves a compatible provider version
Azure constraintsImplement checks for the resource types you useImplement and maintain the catalog your module supportsReuse the catalog of 520 definitions and its existing checks
Planning without Azure accessPossible with pure HCL naming logicPossible with pure HCL naming logicLocal name generation
Trade-offSimple for a narrow convention; repeated logic needs coordinationFlexible, with naming logic and tests to maintainReady-made catalog; adds a provider dependency

For modules with a fixed or specialized convention, accepting a caller-supplied name may be all you need. Global name availability still needs to be checked with Azure.

The Registry showed 31.0 million downloads when I captured the page below on October 24, 2026. That count covers all published versions, repeat installations, and CI runs; one user may account for many downloads.

Terraform Registry screenshot, October 24, 2026. Counts change over time.

What 2.0.0 gave us​

After version 1.2.34, we had accumulated changes that could affect existing configurations:

  • Removing the deprecated azurecaf_naming_convention resource in favor of azurecaf_name.
  • Realigning 64 resource slugs with current CAF abbreviations.
  • Adding 29 AzureRM naming definitions and removing three invalid or obsolete definitions, moving the catalog from 494 to 520 entries.
  • Correcting Azure naming constraints for several resource types.
  • Fixing seeded random generation to use the complete alphabet, which means a previously generated suffix can change.

An altered name can mean replacement of a real Azure resource in a Terraform plan. We developed the migration guide alongside the implementation so users could assess those changes before upgrading.

For v1, we chose a critical-fixes-only maintenance line that preserves existing naming behavior.

The building blocks: GitHub documentation and AzureCAF implementations

I started the release session with:

Lets prepare for v2.0.0

The repository skills gave Copilot procedures for researching naming rules, updating definitions, and testing changes.

For recurring work, we keep Markdown instructions alongside triggers, tools, and permissions, then compile them into .lock.yml workflows for GitHub Actions.

The workflow guide documents the setup, including improvements made after 2.0.0.

The GitHub Agentic Workflows quickstart walks through adding a recurring workflow to a repository. These references pair the general documentation with the files we use in AzureCAF:

Building blockDocumentationAzureCAF implementation
Agent skillsGitHub's guide to agent skillsNaming research skill and provider build/test skill
Workflow structure and compilationHow GitHub Agentic Workflows worksWeekly Azure Sync Markdown source and its compiled Actions workflow
Events, schedules, and filtersAgentic workflow triggersIssue-to-PR workflow, including the new-resource label filter
Permissions and controlled outputsPermissions and safe outputsThe Issue-to-PR source declares its tools, read permissions, and PR/comment outputs
Builds and scheduled testsGitHub Actions documentationProvider CI and nightly regression and AzureRM mock validation
Maintainer activity reportsAgentic workflow quickstartRepo Status workflow
Code review and securityCopilot code review and GitHub Advanced SecurityCodeQL workflow and additional security checks

Being proactive between releases​

The Weekly Azure Sync workflow compares our catalog with tracked AzureRM resources and investigates naming-guidance changes. Issue Triage and Issue Arborist help organize the resulting backlog.

Selected issues labeled new-resource can trigger the Issue-to-PR workflow. It follows the research procedure, updates the catalog, builds the provider, and proposes a PR with supporting sources.

An upstream change can become a research issue before a user reports a failure. Maintainers choose which findings deserve implementation. Each resulting PR should explain its sources, compatibility implications, and remaining uncertainty. Fresh upstream inputs and explicit reporting of incomplete checks are part of maintaining this loop.

A briefing for the maintainer​

The Repo Status workflow gathers recent activity and recommends next steps. It helps me return to the project and decide what to review, investigate, or defer.

When maintenance competes with other commitments, I want a briefing I can act on: the changes awaiting review, the issues behind them, and the next decisions to make. Links to the underlying work let me check a recommendation before committing maintainer time.

Originally daily, it now covers the previous seven days on a weekly schedule. We adjusted the cadence alongside other workflow improvements to keep maintainer attention focused.

Security stays in the review path​

GitHub Advanced Security and other checks supply review evidence: CodeQL scans Go and Actions code; Dependabot security updates, secret scanning, and push protection are enabled. These controls cover agent-prepared changes too. Private-repository availability depends on the relevant GitHub security products.

Where the time went​

To understand where time was spent, I followed Copilot-opened changes from draft PR to review-ready proposal, merge, and publication. The table measures the pace through those stages, using the records available for each milestone.

MeasureMedian elapsed timeSample
Draft PR opened to marked ready for review2h 35m22 PRs with a readiness event
PR opened to merged4.53 days14 merged PRs
Merge to first stable release containing the change3.98 daysThe same 14 merged PRs
PR opened to first stable release containing the change12.03 daysThe same 14 merged PRs

The recorded proposals typically reached review in hours, while the merged changes reached publication in days. These are calendar times, including waiting between steps. The samples differ, so read each median independently.

The merged PRs in this sample shipped in earlier 1.x releases. Human-led, AI-assisted work, including the 2.0.0 preparation, sits outside this Copilot-author timing sample.

The bulk update behind the opening figures shows the work between those milestones. Review removed 16 invalid candidates from the initial proposal. The final change added 89 definitions, taking the catalog from 405 to 494, before publication about 11 days after PR creation.

The 2.0.0 release PR also closed 18 issues with a median age of 497 days, incorporating earlier community work and checking resolutions against the original reports.

Earlier unmarked merged PRs had a median 7.90 days to publication across 99 PRs. Different tasks, periods, and release conditions make that an imperfect baseline. A causal comparison would need comparable work and recorded effort.

Timing definitions and additional case studies

The snapshot covers the public PR history and release records through October 28, 2026. Of 32 Copilot-authored PRs, 14 merged and 18 closed without merging, including superseded or consolidated work. Readiness events were available for 22 PRs. Merge and release medians cover the 14 directly merged PRs; closed, unmerged proposals are excluded from those durations.

Each release is the first published, non-prerelease standard-semver tag containing the merged commit. The medians describe separate distributions and cannot be added together. The earlier unmarked group predates the first visible Copilot PR in May 2025; unrecorded AI assistance remains possible.

The individual timelines vary considerably:

ChangeIssue opened to first review-ready eventPR opened to stable release
Azure Dev Center support10m 20s1h 46m
Dev Center regex correction40m 54s12.08 days
Bulk catalog expansion1h 47m10.98 days

There is a long tail too. The Network Connection Monitor PR was marked ready about 28 hours after opening and took approximately 183 days to reach a release.

Earlier unmarked merged PRs had a median 1.34 days to merge and 7.90 days to publication across 99 PRs. That group predates the first visible Copilot PR in May 2025 and covers different work and release conditions. Some AI use may also be unrecorded. A causal speed comparison would need comparable tasks and a measure of the effort involved.

Building release confidence over time​

Testing was one of the clearest benefits of working with Copilot. The Copilot-coauthored testing work added edge cases and integration checks. Re-running historical provider tests shows statement coverage rising from 82.5% at the earlier baseline to 95.6% in 2.0.0, while named Go test functions grew from 33 to 124.

My confidence built gradually. Reviews and test runs exposed names changing unexpectedly, inputs unavailable during planning, and invalid test fixtures. We investigated each failure, added regression checks, and reran the release gates. That repeated cycle made me more comfortable publishing the release.

The final release evidence included 445 passing AzureRM mock workspaces, plus lifecycle and packaging checks. AI helped us expand and exercise those checks; their results supported the decision to release.

A runnable AzureRM mock-provider example and the local maintenance commands

Historical testing checkpoints​

I reproduced provider-package coverage on isolated historical checkouts using the same go test command and Go 1.27.3:

CheckpointStatement coverageNamed provider test functions
Before the testing expansion82.5%33
After the Copilot-coauthored expansion99.3%61
v2.0.095.6%124

The implementation changed between snapshots: the coverage denominators were 263, 270, and 321 executable statements. The v2 default run passed 117 top-level tests and skipped seven. These counts describe test functions and exercised statements; measuring production reliability would require defect or incident data. Human contributions and production-code changes are part of the comparison.

AzureRM mock-provider example​

A regex test derived from our own catalog can reproduce an error in that catalog, so we also check generated names against AzureRM's configuration validation and exercise the provider lifecycle.

For 2.0.0, the AzureRM v5.0.1 mock sweep covered 445 matching definitions from the 520-entry catalog. The other entries were aliases, non-AzureRM types, or absent from that provider version. All 445 workspaces eventually passed their generated scenarios. Provider-package statement coverage reached 95.6%.

Terraform's mock_provider made that possible without Azure credentials. AzureCAF stayed real; AzureRM was mocked. The mock forwards configuration validation to AzureRM and simulates its planning and apply behavior. AzureRM's real CustomizeDiff hooks, Azure API behavior, and global name availability sit outside the scope of this check.

Lifecycle tests check that a generated name stays stable across creation, subsequent applies, and planning. Testing the published package separately from the local development build also helps us check the delivery path.

Live Azure acceptance and deployment behavior require their own integration checks.

Here is a reduced, runnable example using the released providers. It requires Terraform 1.7 or later. I added the override variable to demonstrate the negative control below.

# main.tf
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.7.0"

  required_providers {
    azurecaf = {
      source  = "aztfmod/azurecaf"
      version = "= 2.0.0"
    }
    azurerm = {
      source  = "hashicorp/azurerm"
      version = "= 5.0.1"
    }
  }
}

provider "azurecaf" {}

provider "azurerm" {
  features {}
  subscription_id = "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000"
}

variable "azurerm_name_override" {
  type    = string
  default = null
}

resource "azurecaf_name" "example" {
  name          = "myproject"
  resource_type = "azurerm_resource_group"
  prefixes      = ["prod"]
  clean_input   = true
}

resource "azurerm_resource_group" "example" {
  name     = coalesce(var.azurerm_name_override, azurecaf_name.example.result)
  location = "westeurope"
}

output "result" {
  value = azurecaf_name.example.result
}
# tests/validate.tftest.hcl
mock_provider "azurerm" {}

run "validate_generated_name" {
  command = apply

  assert {
    condition     = output.result != ""
    error_message = "AzureCAF returned an empty name."
  }

  assert {
    condition     = length(output.result) >= 1 && length(output.result) <= 90
    error_message = "The resource group name must contain 1 to 90 characters."
  }

  assert {
    condition     = can(regex("^[a-zA-Z0-9-._\\(\\)]{0,89}[a-zA-Z0-9-_\\(\\)]$", output.result))
    error_message = "The name does not match the CAF resource group definition."
  }

  assert {
    condition     = azurerm_resource_group.example.name == azurecaf_name.example.result
    error_message = "The AzureRM resource name must match the AzureCAF result."
  }
}

run "second_apply" {
  command = apply

  assert {
    condition     = output.result == run.validate_generated_name.result
    error_message = "The generated name changed on the second apply."
  }
}

run "replan" {
  command = plan

  assert {
    condition     = output.result == run.validate_generated_name.result
    error_message = "The generated name changed during the next plan."
  }
}

The later runs reuse the test file's state and check the name after a second apply and another plan. These assertions cover name stability within the mock test. Verifying a real Azure deployment's lifecycle requires a live integration test.

Run the example in a fresh directory with the following CLI configuration. Direct Registry installation isolates this check from local development overrides and implicit filesystem mirrors:

# registry.tfrc
provider_installation {
  direct {}
}
TF_CLI_CONFIG_FILE="$PWD/registry.tfrc" terraform init
TF_CLI_CONFIG_FILE="$PWD/registry.tfrc" \
  terraform test -filter=tests/validate.tftest.hcl -verbose

For a negative control, pass an invalid name directly to the AzureRM resource:

TF_CLI_CONFIG_FILE="$PWD/registry.tfrc" \
  TF_VAR_azurerm_name_override='invalid!name' \
  terraform test -filter=tests/validate.tftest.hcl

This command should fail with an AzureRM name-validation diagnostic. That failure confirms AzureRM's configuration validation is active in the test.

Testing the provider we were actually changing​

The release harness tested the AzureCAF binary built from our changes. Each generated workspace had a CLI configuration like this, using an absolute directory containing terraform-provider-azurecaf:

# terraform.rc
provider_installation {
  dev_overrides {
    "aztfmod/azurecaf" = "/absolute/path/to/local-provider-build"
  }
  direct {}
}

The runner isolated provider installation during terraform init, then verified and activated the local override for terraform test. In the provider repository, these targets perform the build, setup, generation, and execution:

make test_mock_azurerm_changed
make test_mock_azurerm_all

The generator supplies default, prefixed, and seeded-random naming variations, plus the other arguments needed for each resource's configuration validation. The results apply to those fixtures and the provider version used.

Keep the automation worth running​

The no-op tracker recorded 401 reports from distinct runs between June 11 and September 9, 2026; 251 came from Issue-to-PR. Some explicitly reported unrelated labels. Clean health checks can be useful; those irrelevant event-triggered runs showed where filtering needed attention.

We used that feedback to refine the process. After the release, aztfmod/terraform-provider-azurecaf#936 moved predictable test jobs into ordinary scheduled Actions and tightened agent triggers or reduced their frequency.

Agents remain useful for research, interpretation, and proposed changes. Their schedules and outputs need the same attention as other automation. The tracker measures activity; financial cost would require billing data.

One release incident that exposed the difference between instructions and controls

The first Release Labeler run failed on a missing v2.0.0 label. Its instructions assumed the tool could create labels; the safe-output configuration required them to exist already. Applying release labels also started unrelated issue-agent runs because their label check happened after activation.

This excerpt from the Issue-to-PR workflow's frontmatter shows the label filter before agent activation and the permitted PR output. The full source also configures the agent's tools and permissions:

on:
  issues:
    types: [labeled]
    names: [new-resource]

safe-outputs:
  create-pull-request:
    title-prefix: "[auto] "
    labels: [automated, new-resource]

The task description, trigger, and permitted outputs all need to agree.

A frame from the release recording showing the failure at the safe-output step.

aztfmod/terraform-provider-azurecaf#929 subsequently tightened the triggers, output configuration, release metadata checks, and failure propagation. We now have additional checks for how the automation starts, applies outputs, and reports failures.

Turning capacity into outcomes​

A researched proposal gives me useful preparation capacity. A richer test suite gives me more evidence for review. Both help, and both still need maintainer time, prioritization, and a path to release. The timestamps show the elapsed time; understanding each delay takes further investigation.

I would read enterprise AI productivity figures the same way. More prepared changes can increase the queue at an already-busy review or integration stage. Realizing the benefit also depends on approvals, rollout windows, and adoption by users.

For engineering leaders, I would follow three measures together:

  • Preparation: time to a review-ready change, including the rework needed to make it acceptable.
  • Delivery: time through review, integration, and release, with attention to growing queues.
  • Outcomes: whether users adopt the change and receive the intended benefit.

In AzureCAF, publication is the milestone we can observe. User adoption and production reliability would need their own evidence.

If changes wait for review, the next improvement might be clearer PR evidence, smaller changes, or protected reviewer time. If they wait after merge, look at release preparation and rollout constraints. Tracking the handoffs helps a team choose an investment that can move delivery forward.

Trying 2.0.0: installation and migration examples

For a new configuration, this example uses the azurecaf_name data source without any Azure deployment:

terraform {
  required_providers {
    azurecaf = {
      source  = "aztfmod/azurecaf"
      version = "~> 2.0"
    }
  }
}

data "azurecaf_name" "example" {
  name          = "myproject"
  resource_type = "azurerm_resource_group"
  prefixes      = ["prod"]
  suffixes      = ["001"]
}

output "resource_group_name" {
  value = data.azurecaf_name.example.result
}

~> 2.0 allows compatible 2.x releases; use = 2.0.0 to reproduce that exact version.

For an existing configuration, read the v2.0.0 migration guide before upgrading. Migrate azurecaf_naming_convention while still on v1.x, record existing names, and review the complete plan. The azurecaf_name resource supports passthrough mode when you need to retain an existing name:

resource "azurecaf_name" "current" {
  name          = "stdevmyapp001"
  resource_type = "azurerm_storage_account"
  passthrough   = true
}

Complete the guide's import and reference-update steps to migrate the old state before removing the legacy resource.

Now it's your turn​

Start with one recurring maintenance task, give it a clear output and owner, and follow it through review and release. Leave the useful checks and procedures in the repository for the next run. Then use the delivery data to decide where to spend the next hour.

The AzureCAF workflows and release notes are public. Happy to hear what you find!

Thanks,

Arnaud

item.content:encoded:
Microsoft Cloud Adoption Framework for Azure Terraform edition, helps you deploy resources on Azure in a structured way, it come with various components that you can leverage together or you can pick based on where you are on the cloud journey and based on your needs.

Today we are going to review how to contribute to the Cloud Adoption Framework for Azure Terraform module Open Source project.

The CAF module​

Almost a year ago we switched to a one-module approach that allows high speed of evolution (we know how time-consuming it is to update a set of small modules). We have implemented that with conditional submodules feature introduced in Terraform 0.13 and we have been running that way up to Terraform 1.0.0 with excellent feedbacks.

Having one single module makes the development more difficult for the developer, as it requires working on the iterative structures and junction between the different objects – One could argue this is the job of anyone trying to put more than two Terraform modules together. On the other hand, having the single module integrated allows composition and configuration way faster for the DevOps engineers and architects putting together a configuration.

This module can be leveraged from any Terraform code via the Terraform registry, using the following syntax:

module "caf" {
  source  = "aztfmod/caf/azurerm"
  version = "5.3.11"
  # insert the 6 required variables here
}

You can find many examples on the module GitHub repository here.

The power of the community​

With the speed of evolution of Terraform and the Azure provider, inner-sourcing components for enterprises is a pragmatic option that allows DevOps engineers to focus on delivering value.

Adding a new capability​

Let’s say you are reviewing the CAF module capabilities and realise it’s missing a feature, and you want to write it and contribute to the community.

We will do that with a simple example: someone in the community opened an issue for Azure Dedicated Hosts, which allows you to deploy a dedicated Hypervisor for your Virtual Machines. You can find all the details about it here:

Basically we will create two objects:

  • the hosts groups: a set of machines in a particular region with a set of capabilities like availability sones and fault domains:
  • the hosts: the hypervisor itself, which will be hosting the Virtual Machines.

And we can foresee that we will need to change the virtual machines module capabilities to declare that a particular VM will be deployed on a dedicated host.

The toolset​

In order to get things started, I will get the following development environment:

  • GitHub Codespace
    • Codespace allows me to develop directly off my browser. I can fork the repo, then I don’t even need to clone it locally. Since the module has a .devcontainer it will pick the right version of development environment plus the development tools I need.
      I could also clone the project it and then open it locally into Visual Studio Code, the same development environment would have been created.
  • Terraform documentation
    • For Azure Dedicated Host, I browse off the Terraform registry and find the following related components:
      • https://registry.terraform.io/providers/hashicorp/azurerm/latest/docs/resources/dedicated_host
      • https://registry.terraform.io/providers/hashicorp/azurerm/latest/docs/resources/dedicated_host_group
  • Azure subscription
    • You can get started for free here: https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/free/

Aligning all side-by-side, and lets go for the coding!

For the rest, let’s do it in a video – full screen required :):

Refactoring and dependencies​

It’s very rare that we get things right from the beginning, so after a review, I detect that I can improve the following ones:

Object syntax for the VM​

In my initial implementation, I did the following syntax to reference the Dedicated Host to my virtual machine:

 dedicated_host_group = {
        dedicated_host_group_key = "dh1"
        # lz_key = "remoteLZKey"
        # id = "full resource ID"
    }

But I actually don’t the need group but the host, so I refactor the object and standardize on our pattern that allow using the object from:

  • resource ID of the object deployed outside of this module
  • key of an object deployed locally
  • key of an object from another landing zone (via the lz_key attribute)
  dedicated_host = {
        key = "dh1"
        # lz_key = "remoteLZKey"
        # id = "full resource ID"
    }

Composition patterns to retrieve the Dedicated VM dedicated​

At first the pattern to locate the dedicated host_id in the VM object was the following:

dedicated_host_id = try(try(each.value.dedicated_host_group.id, var.dedicated_hosts[try(each.value.dedicated_host_group.lz_key, var.client_config.landingzone_key)][each.value.dedicated_host_group.dedicated_host_group_key].id), null)

It worked, but did not align with updated patterns that offer better visibility and troubleshooting, so I just updated it into:

dedicated_host_id = try(coalesce(
    try(each.value.dedicated_host.id, null),
    var.dedicated_hosts[try(each.value.dedicated_host.lz_key, var.client_config.landingzone_key)][each.value.dedicated_host.key].id,
    ),
    null
  )

Dependencies​

There are also dependencies that I managed in the meantime, like the name convention provider. I checked at the naming reference here.

The CAF Terraform name provider can be found on the Terraform registry here

And we load it this way:

terraform {
  required_providers {
    azurecaf = {
      source  = "aztfmod/azurecaf"
      version = "~> 1.2.0"
    }
}

It was my first PR to the name provider so I was quite surprised of the easiness of contribution, the most complicated part was to find the right regex to match the supported characters for Azure Dedicated Hosts.

You can review the PR here and contribution guide.

Now it’s your turn​

Let’s get started! Happy to hear your thoughts and learn from your feedbacks, also if you identify a missing feature and you want to give it a try, lets:

  1. In the GitHub Issues, verify if there is an Epic covering the module you are describing.
  2. If the change you are proposing is a sub-feature of an epic, please open an issue describing your changes in details and the reasons for the change with an example.
  3. On submitting the PR, please mention the Issue related to the PR.

Also before submitting the PR, make sure:

  1. Make sure you are using the Visual Studio Dev environment with pre-commit hooks effective.
  2. Matching with coding conventions and common engineering criteria described here.
  3. Provide examples including the main scenarios the module is supposed to achieve.
  4. Include integration tests for your examples.

Thanks

Arnaud

item.description: More than a year ago we announced at Ignite 2019 that Cloud Adoption Framework proposes an implementation on Terraform. Since then, we have seen a tremendous feedbacks from customers and partners architects. In the meantime lot of great things have happened: an enterprise-scale reference architectur
item.content:encoded:
More than a year ago we announced at Ignite 2019 that Cloud Adoption Framework proposes an implementation on Terraform. Since then, we have seen a tremendous feedbacks from customers and partners architects.

In the meantime lot of great things have happened: an enterprise-scale reference architecture and it’s ARM-based implementation, alongside with an incredible acceleration on the release rhythm of the Azure Terraform provider reducing the delay between features appearing in Azure and time it is available in native Terraform.

Terraform 0.13​

Terraform 0.13 has been released mid August, and you can read the full details here. For us, the major improvements are:

  • Registry-based provider sourcing: No more need to side-load our custom provider, you can leverage it directly from the Terraform registry just like we for modules: our CAF provider is published here
  • Variables validation: Only allow variable to be within a certain range or validating a regex.
  • Iterations and conditions on modules: more later in this article.

Testing Terraform 0.13 with rover​

After weeks of testing reliability of Terraform 0.13 during this summer’s beta, we were very happy with the stability and performance so we decided to push further our way of operating.

rover is part of the DevOps toolset we provide you with and recommend using for development teams and pipelines deployment. During this testing stage, it played full role allowing us to switch fast from one codebase to the other and also to one version of Terraform to the other.

What’s new in CAF landing zones​

Leveraging Terraform 0.13, we were able to introduce new concepts in landing zones on Azure:

One module to rule them all​

We have been curating 20+ modules during the last year, all published on the Terraform registry and some of them being consumed more than 26,000 times.

While it was important to have different modules to maintain a very fine-grained versioning of the components we use, we found it to be a lot of work, for little added value.

We then decided to explore a model where we use only one module, that would call and iterate on different submodules – that permitted by Terraform 0.13.

We must admit we have been impressed by the results on how the graph performs, and the speed at which it works.

So the new module is still in preview but already available available here https://registry.terraform.io/modules/aztfmod/caf/azurerm/latest

Iteration-based objects deployment​

To deploy core features, landing zones are now calling one module. This master module has all the major components we need to deploy within landing zones, and it iterates on every objects in the following way:

So from the configuration prospective, you define your network configuration with a complex object like this one:

So wether you need one or ten virtual networks, we iterate automatically for you.
By default the vnets like all the other variables are set to {}. So it means nothing will be created, only the variables you populate will be iterated on.

Key-based configuration and customization​

All configuration objects will call each other based on the object keys. As we just seen, we use complex objects that are iterated and referenced via their keys.

It means for instance we create all the resource groups using the following object:

In that example, we create two resource groups which keys are vnet_region1 and vnet_region2. We we create the virtual network called hub (and which key is hub_sg we reference the resource group via the resource_group_key property.

Under the hood, the module is mapping back the resource group to the key with the following logic:

No-code environment composition​

Overall this makes writing the modules code slightly more complicated, but what it means for users is the possibility to compose complex environment without changing anything in the code.

A good example for that is the networking landing zone where we are able to compose all kind of Azure network topologies (like Hub-and-Spokes virtual networks, Virtual WAN-based hub-and-spokes, etc.).

We can establish peering between on object in the current landing zone and a remote landing zones (this is very common to have separate states for the hub and the spokes)

Overall we have tested it internally and externally and have found:

  • We have been able to compose any kind of architecture using this pattern.
  • It is very fast to compose a new environment.
  • It is very fast to process by Terraform and Terraform graph.

DevOps from the ground-up​

At the root of deployments, we have our launchpad which sets the Azure backend and collaboration requirements.

We want to offer our customers choices and options so the new launchpad is modular: allowing add-ons to complement the configuration like:

  • DevOps Pipelines configuration and secret management leveraging the official Microsoft Azure DevOps provider for Terraform
  • Terraform Cloud and Terraform Enterprise
  • GitHub and GitHub Enterprise
  • Any other solution.

For an example of landing zones on Azure DevOps, you can refer to the following demo:

For an example of landing zones on Terraform Cloud, you can refer to the following demo:

Coding everywhere​

Using Visual Studio Codespaces or GitHub Codespaces, you can develop and deploy landing zones without installing anything on your laptop, with full access to the rover and development environment.

You can try it now: or on GitHub Codespaces

The journey ahead​

Enterprise-scale landing zones​

Enterprise-scale is a reference architecture, set of design guidelines, and reference implementation for an Azure enterprise environment.
You can find all the details here..

We are working on it with the team and are integrating the module on the foundations layers. You can also try out the module here.

Delivering solutions​

We found a lot of interest from customers and partners to leverage the DevOps and everything-as-code environment we setup in order to accelerate the development and the deployment of ready-to-use solutions.

We are currently working to publish solutions that you can stack-up on top of the lower levels of landing zones, amongst them, you will be able to find:
* AKS topologies including layer 4 applications
* Data and analytics, to deploy Azure Synapse, Databricks, Machine Learning, etc..
* More to come…

On the way to Terraform 0.14​

Just announced, Terraform 0.14 will also bring some good features, you will be able to test it out soon in a new rover. You can read the news here

Contribute​

All of that is still work in progress and you can contribute by opening an issue, a pull request or just testing it!

The repo is here: https://github.com/Azure/caf-terraform-landingzones and (most) of the things described are currently in the 0.4 branch, and will be available on this month release (2010 Update)

We’d love to hear from you, so don’t hesitate to give us feedback here or on Gitter

Arnaud

item.content:encoded:
At Microsoft Ignite 2019, we announced that Cloud Adoption Framework for Azure now has a Terraform edition of it’s landing zones. We see landing zones as a great way to enable value quicker on Azure, and as we see tremendous excitment and growth in this area, we are evolving the experience to make it simpler and more powerful.

Adopting CAF landing zones with Terraform, customer consistenly realize they can:

  • deploy foundations of cloud environments fast
  • easily deploy governance and policies as code (with ongoing compliance enforcement and remediation)
  • have consistent ways to deploy innovation (infra as code, policies as code or application code are using the same mechanisms).
  • and many more.

This overall enables them to: optimize their operations, innovate faster and cheaper, but we will come back to that in another article.

For now, let’s get you started with landing zones development and deployment!

When deploying Infra-As-Code environments, we found it extremely important to have:

  • strong versioning (accross dev environment, DevOps pipelines, etc.).
  • short feedback loops: ability to innovate fast on your development, test new code without having to go through the whole pull-request and so mechanisms.
  • accomodate diversity of environments (running Windows, Mac, Linux).
  • strong identity consistency and no secret in any code.

In order to enable that, we use Docker containers as development (on your laptop) and deployment (CI/CD pipelines) environement. The toolset is packaged inside what we called the rover and in order to get started – whichever your platform is, just:

  • Install Docker
  • Install Visual Studio Code

Once its done, make sure Docker is up and running, then Open Visual Studio Code:

We need to install “Remote Development” extension, so click the Extensions icon and then find and install “Remote Development” from Microsoft:

To make your life easier, we are going to leverage Visual Studio Development Containers, which allows you to seamlessly work on your machine and execute your code in the rover container.:

So on your machine, you will have your Terraform files, with your Git connection and other tools, but when you run the code, its seemlessly integrated with the Rover running in the container, so you can develop, test, run the complete environment.

Deploying your first landing zone

Once you have deployed the prerequisites, you can just clone (with Git, or GitHub Desktop) from our repository: http://aka.ms/tf-landingzones and open it in Visual Studio.

If you look at the files, it’s classic Terraform scripts except for the  .devcontainer folder where we have two files:

  • devcontainer.json: describes how to connect to the container, the mounting points and extensions.
  • docker-compose.yml: describes the container configuration needed, especially where to get the rover image (tip: we put it on the Docker registry so you dont have to manage it)

You can then go to the bottom left, green part of Visual Studio Code and select

Open Remote-Containers: Open Workspace in Container, then select the default workspace we created for you (workspace.code-workspace). You will see a new window opening and you can see the details of the Docker container operations:

  • downloading the container from registry
  • mounting the volumes
  • creating the network
  • installing VSCode drivers in the containers

You are now ready to start hacking, you can start by launching:

  1. rover login 
  2. rover /tf/caf/landingzones/landingzone_caf_foundations plan 
  3. rover /tf/caf/landingzones/landingzone_caf_foundations apply 

So let the fun begin!

item.content:encoded:
This article describes the old experience for Azure CAF landing zones on Terraform, please refer to this article for the new updated experience:

https://arnaud-web.azurewebsites.net/2019/11/15/cloud-adoption-framework-landing-zones-with-terraform/

Cloud Adoption Framework for Azure has a great set of recommendations to accelerate deployment of Azure for entreprises who seek to consolidate their IT environment in the cloud and innovate on their applications.

CAF introduces landing zones as a concept that describes all the elements that must be in place to deploy a production-grade quality deployment (ie, that includes a minimal set of auditing, controls, policies, etc).

In order to accelerate that, let’s review how to deploy our first landing zone for Azure based on Terraform! We assume that you know Terraform and Azure already, if thats not the case, spend some time on my previous post.

We have published and will keep on updating a repository on GitHub: http://aka.ms/tf-landingzones

Getting started​

The fastest way is to use Azure Cloud Shell:

  1. Open https://shell.azure.com
  2. Go to the clouddrive directory: cd clouddrive
  3. Clone the GitHub repo from http://aka.ms/tf-landingzones git clone https://github.com/aztfmod/blueprints.git
  4. Initialize the environment – this will create the fundamentals for the Terraform state, like Storage Account, Azure Key Vault, and the managed identities: ./launchpad.sh
  5. Deploy your first tranquility blueprint: ./launchpad.sh landingzone_vdc_level1 plan
  6. Review the configuration and if you are ok with it, deploy it by running: ./launchpad.sh landingzone_vdc_level1 apply

Below is a quick demo of doing that:

Customization​

In order to ease your first contact with the landing zone, we created a sample configuration file proto.landing_zone_vdc_level1.auto.tfvars. As any .auto.tfvars file, it is going to be picked up automatically by Terraform when running. This file automatically configures all variables needed to get started:

  • Retention period for Activity logs, and operations logs.
  • Names of the resource groups to be created.
  • Location of the resources to be deployed.
  • Tags for the resources.
  • Name of log analytics and list of solutions to be deployed.
  • Security center contact details.

You can tune it to match your criteria, we hope the syntax is self explanatory, feel free to provide feedback on it!

Quick tour of the architecture:​

Currently the solution is composed of 3 main components:

1. Launchpad.sh​

Is a shell script, it initiates the Terraform state locally, uploads it to the Azure storage account, manages the environment variables and communication accross landing zones and other components.

2. Level0_launchpad​

Creates a Key Vault, an Azure managed identity a storage account that is used to create store the Terraform state of our environment. It also creates a serie of service principals to be used to access the Terraform state and to integrate with Azure DevOps (in a future release). For full documentation, refer to the readme file.

3. Landingzone_vdc_level1​

This vdc level1 landing zones leverages one blueprint (called tranquility) that sets the foundation for everything accounting and operations logs in your Azure subscription:

  • Resource groups

  • Activity Logging

  • Diagnostics Logging

  • Log Analytics

item.description: <Updated 11th July 2019> Since we started to help customers of all sizes to deploy cloud technologies, we have developed many frameworks which all evolved in parallel over time. You may have heard about: Cloud Adoption Framework, Cloud Operations Model, Entreprise Cloud Strategy, Entreprise Sc
item.content:encoded:
<Updated 11th July 2019>

Since we started to help customers of all sizes to deploy cloud technologies, we have developed many frameworks which all evolved in parallel over time. You may have heard about: Cloud Adoption Framework, Cloud Operations Model, Entreprise Cloud Strategy, Entreprise Scaffolding and maybe a couple more.

The CAF is dead, long live the CAF!​

A couple of weeks ago, we published a new version of CAF – Cloud Adoption Framework for Azure, which consolidates all of our engineering and field best practices, as well as patterns that we’ve seen from big entreprises going to the cloud.

CAF has now five main sections which guide you throughout the whole circle:

  1. Plan
  2. Ready
  3. Migrate
  4. Manage
  5. Govern

This model is very realistic and field inspired, including some discussions around adoption with one or more cloud providers.

Governance​

One of the most intimidating aspects of cloud adoption is the governance: how to manage new risks that are involved with cloud deployments and how to accompany that with entreprise processes and policies (and how does it remain current).

It is of course an iterative process that will evolve as you add new services into your environment: from dev/test to prod, and from legacy 3-tiers application to a brand new cloud-native application.

We distinguish 5 disciplines in governance:

  1. Cost management
  2. Security baseline
  3. Resource consistency
  4. Identity baseline
  5. Deployment Acceleration

But the difficulty is the first step: how do I get a minimal viable product (MVP) for my first cloud deployment?

Actions: In order to avoid you the blank page syndrome, we have prepared you some actions:

  1. Determine your immediate objectives with cloud, and the readiness of your organization. Cloud Assessment Tool: https://aka.ms/CAF/gov/assess 
  2. Establish your governance MVP:
    1. Small to Medium Entreprises
    2. Large Entreprises

For all those journey we document a minimum viable product across the five disciplines, we explain the design decisions we took for you, the discussion points and alternative design considerations.

When we define governance, we also think about compliance to the rules, and automatic remediation methods for it: this is called Azure Policy.

Along the way, if you are going for ongoing compliance, why not going to continuous integration and continuous deployment for your infrastructure?

If you want to have a look at all of that in action, check at:

  • Our webinar on Azure Cloud and Compliance
  • Infra as Code hands-on-labs – https://www.azuredevopslabs.com/labs/vstsextend/terraform/ 

Azure Scaffolding​

We used to talk a lot of  “scaffolding” as it is an excellent checklist, or set of mandatory technical implentation details for a good cloud deployment. It is being replaced by the “landing zone” construct (see next section).

Here is a refresher picture about what scaffolding includes:

Important readings on Azure Scaffolding:

  • the documentation: https://docs.microsoft.com/en-gb/azure/architecture/cloud-adoption/appendix/azure-scaffold 
  • an example: https://docs.microsoft.com/en-gb/azure/architecture/cloud-adoption/appendix/azure-scaffold-examples 

Azure Landing Zones​

Landing Zone is our new construct to describe a good deployment, its replacing the scaffolding idea but takes all of its good ideas.

It has the idea of primitives which includes all mandatory decisions:

  • Management Groups
  • Resource Groups
  • Naming Standards
  • Number of subscriptions

On the technical implementations of Governance it includes all of:

  • Policies
  • Cost
  • Monitoring
  • Identity

Moreover, it comes with all set of decision trees in order to help you when it comes to implementation with your customers/partners:

  • Compute decisions
  • Storage decisions
  • Networking decisions
  • Database decisions

Azure Virtual Datacenter​

Azure VDC is a set of concepts, implentation guidance and automation scripts that allows you to build a highly available and highly secure datacenter, based on Microsoft Azure services.

You can find all the materials here: https://docs.microsoft.com/en-gb/azure/architecture/vdc/ 

Check at the automation scripts and all the archetypes that allow you to deploy a VDC environment fast – based on Docker and Python : https://github.com/Azure/vdc

As last reference, as usual, our Azure Architecture Center

That’s it, now you will have a very well architected Azure deployment!

Arnaud
